implementation_notes: Python's canonical realization is the Borg idiom: keep one class-level dictionary and rebind each instance's __dict__ to it in __init__ (self.__dict__ = self._shared_state), so attribute writes on any instance land in the same storage while identity (a is b) stays distinct - Alex Martelli's recipe, and the reason Python practitioners call the pattern Borg. What replaces the classic structure is the attribute dictionary itself: there is no static member to declare, only the shared mapping, and because the rebinding goes through self, a subclass that assigns its own _shared_state gets a separate state (the documented data override). Prefer Borg when instances should stay ordinary attribute bags.
pitfalls: The __dict__ rebinding does not work for classes with __slots__, subclasses of built-in types, or types that override __getattribute__/__setattr__; those need explicit delegation instead.
Identity stays distinct while state does not: a is b is False and a == b is False by default, yet writes leak across every instance - define __eq__/__hash__ deliberately or document the asymmetry.
The shared dict lives as long as the process: tests inherit each other's attributes unless a reset helper clears _shared_state in teardown.

variants.name: Class attribute as the shared slot (plain class variable)
variants.idiom_name: class variable written via type(self).level = value
variants.implementation_notes: A plain class attribute is already shared by every instance: write it explicitly on the class (type(self).level = value) and every instance's read sees the new value, while a bare self.level = ... would shadow it with a private attribute - exactly the behaviour to avoid here. This is the simplest realization and needs no __init__ trick; it fits monostates whose state is a small fixed set of fields and changes the inheritance semantics relative to Borg: a subclass that writes through type(self) gets its own class attribute, so each subclass becomes its own monostate unless the write targets the base class explicitly.
variants.code_sketch:
class LogSettings:
    level: int = 1                    # class variable: one slot

    def set_level(self, value: int) -> None:
        type(self).level = value      # never self.level = ... (shadows)

s = LogSettings()
s.set_level(3)
print(LogSettings().level)            # 3
pitfalls: Assigning self.level = value creates an instance attribute that shadows the class variable, and the monostate property silently breaks for that instance; always write through the class.
Mutable class attributes (list, dict) are shared by in-place mutation but replaced by assignment - pick one discipline and document it.
Inheritance changes the target: type(self).level in a subclass writes the subclass's own attribute, unless the code deliberately writes BaseClass.level.
